summary: Manager one-to-one between Chris Klevan and Richard Claessen, held immediately before the daily sales team meeting. The first half is personal-state coaching: Richard describes working on his own reactivity, listening to 'Letting Go' on Audible and sitting with his thoughts, and Chris walks him through a mindfulness practice of dropping the story and staying with the bodily sensation. Richard shares that his personal target is $10k/month, driven by a goal of buying his father a Tudor watch after three consecutive $10k months. The second half is a call review: they open the recording of a call Richard had just lost, with a prospect named Frank in Jersey City set by Kim, and watch the moments where it went wrong. Chris diagnoses that the prospect had boxed the offer as ordinary online coaching from early on and was never moved out of that frame, so by the time price landed he was pricing features rather than a transformation. Chris also corrects a specific claim Richard made about Trevor's availability. The session ends with Chris going to let the rest of the team into the meeting.
notable: Richard made a claim about Trevor's availability on the live Frank call that Chris told him he cannot make. On the replayed audio Richard says one-to-ones happen "whenever it's needed. So it's not like a specific every week, every month or anything. It comes down to when it's actually needed. Everything is done through the SMS, so he's constantly..." Chris interrupts: "He's also not sure. He doesn't just... for lots of people." Richard: "I know. Like, the first time I said it, I don't even know why I said it. But, yeah, I know it's not..." Chris: "Yeah, can't say that." Richard then says: "Maybe it's good that I didn't close him then."

Chris Klevan's stated position on qualification is unusually strong for a sales manager and worth recording as company policy: "Nobody needs coaching", "I'm not here to convince you to do coaching", and if the prospect cannot say what would make hiring a coach a good decision, "okay, cool. Like, well, why don't you go and figure that out? And then we'll have another call if you decide this is something you want to do."

Richard identifies his own error as challenging a prospect on whether he needed coaching at all: "Why would I even challenge him on it? Like, it's up to him if he wants coaching. I don't need to challenge him on needing coaching."

Richard dropped the price under time pressure created by the prospect and knew at the time it was premature: "So that's where I let myself fall and where I went into price, which I probably shouldn't have done at that point already." The prospect then left the call before any objection handling: "he was like, oh, we're going in circles now. I've got to go. Bye."
Richard believes the prospect's stated reason for leaving was untrue: "he had a call at 12, but this call ended at 11, so that was probably just an excuse to make it quick."

The lost prospect Frank has a material injury history that came through the setter notes: "His hour and a half to two hour isolated workouts are plateauing and risk re-injury" and "He's had trainers in the past that overestimated his capacity, causing setbacks, he got injured. He wants a safe structured plan that respects his injury history." Kim set the call.
Chris confirms the internal term 'price drop' means revealing the price, not discounting: "When did you, do you know around what time you dropped price?"

Recording hygiene is managed manually and deliberately: "I'm going to kick out the Fathom so we can get fresh ones" — sessions are split into separate recordings by the manager, which explains adjacent files on the same day.

Chris coaches call-review methodology that the audit should know exists: track all calls, find the objections that recur most often, work backwards from them, and alter the questions that consistently land badly.
